vignette:
Elena came to therapy at twenty-one, a year after she had graduated from art school and begun working as a junior animator for a small studio. She sat forward on the edge of the chair, her hands clasped tightly in her lap, and spoke in a low, rapid voice as though she needed to get the story out before she lost her nerve.

The event that had shaped her, she said, was not one single moment but a decade of them. From the time she was seven until she was seventeen, her father had thrown things at her mother. Elena had watched from doorways, from behind the sofa, from the top of the stairs. She remembered the sound of a ceramic vase shattering against the kitchen wall, the smell of the dust from the drywall it had punched through, the way her mother would stand very still afterward, not crying, not moving, as though staying frozen might make her invisible. No one had ever been held accountable. Her father still lived in the same city. Her mother had never pressed charges. Elena had learned early that the world did not correct itself, and that bad things simply happened and kept happening.

Now, as an adult, she found herself living inside the echo of those years. Her memories of the worst incidents did not feel like memories at all. They felt more real than the present moment. When she thought about her father's face contorted in rage, she could smell the faint metallic tang of blood from the time her mother's lip had split, or the dusty smell of the living room rug where she had crouched, pressing her hands over her ears. She would try to push the memory away before it fully arrived-she had developed a skill for slamming a mental door on an image before it could play out-but she was not always fast enough. When she failed, the memory consumed her, and she would find herself trembling in her chair at work, the animation software still open on her screen, her colleagues unaware.

Her triggers were everywhere. At the studio, a coworker tossed a stress ball across the room to another desk, and Elena's entire body locked. Her heart slammed against her ribs, and she had to excuse herself to the bathroom, where she stood with her hands braced on the sink, telling herself she was safe, she was an adult, no one was throwing anything at her. She had become hypervigilant to movement in her peripheral vision; any sudden motion-a hand raised to wave, a chair pushed back too quickly-made her flinch as though she were about to be struck. Her startle response was so pronounced that she had snapped at a colleague who had simply walked up behind her desk. She had been irritable for months, short-tempered with everyone, and she knew it was costing her friendships, but she could not seem to stop the angry words that came out of her mouth before she could think.

To manage the chaos she felt inside, Elena had begun to control the one thing she could: food. She restricted her eating with rigid precision, counting calories, skipping meals, telling herself that if she could govern her own body with enough discipline, she would not be helpless. But the belief that she could not cope with even the slightest upset persisted. A small frustration-a file that would not render, a bus that was late-sent her into a spiral of despair. She was certain that she could not handle anything, that she was fundamentally incapable of managing her own life.

She had also stopped making plans. When friends asked if she wanted to grab dinner next week or see a movie in two months, she felt a cold dread. Making a plan felt like tempting fate, like assuming the future existed when she knew, deep down, that it did not. She avoided anything that reminded her of her father-certain songs, certain brands of beer, the particular shade of gray of a sedan like his-and she had deleted all the old family photos from her phone, but she could not delete the images from her mind.

What finally brought Elena to therapy was a morning at work when a coworker, trying to be friendly, had shown her a photo from a recent family gathering. The flash of a smiling group, the warmth of a living room, had triggered a memory so vivid that Elena had stood up, walked out of the building, and sat on a bench in the parking lot, shaking, for twenty minutes. She knew she could not keep living this way. She was afraid that she would never feel safe, that the past would always be more real than the present. But she was also, for the first time, hoping that someone might show her how to stop running from a memory that would not stay locked away.
